title: AI-Driven Terraform: Move Fast Without Losing Control
story_key: story|title:ai driven terraform move fast without losing control
content_excerpt: Having AI write IaC is no longer unusual. It can add a module, change a few resources, and draft policy much faster than a person. That speed brings a different problem. A change can pull in unrelated resources. Terraform that is perfectly valid can still delete or replace resources, or loosen permissions. Those issues are not always obvious in code review. As the volume grows, reviewing every line by hand stops scaling. Handing the review to another AI adds another opinion, not another guarantee. The real question is this: how can AI keep writing and iterating while its mistakes are caught consistently and kept out of production? I reduce it to three steps: define what AI may change, verify the result with scripts and policy, then leave production writes to human approval and CI/CD. Within that scope, AI can generate code, make small commits, and revise its work from concrete errors. Scripts check formatting, syntax, change scope, and plan risk. Policy checks infrastructure rules. Repository changes and production writes follow separate paths. AI may change code on a controlled branch. A person approves merges, live policy changes, and production changes; CI/CD performs the approved operation. AI does not need to be limited to a few lines, but every task needs a clear scope. If the task is to adjust one database connection, it should not also change unrelated resources or refactor a module. These checks do not require a model to understand the business context, and their result should not depend on how the model interprets them. Local checks give AI a quick feedback loop. CI provides the final gate. Reusing the same scripts and rules in both places avoids changes that pass locally and fail under a different standard after submission. Formatting and syntax only cover the code layer. Policy should manage the rules that govern infrastructure security and platform standards. If the current environment supports tfpolicy , existing rules can move over gradually. The toolset can converge over time, but rule migration still needs semantic equivalence. Merge duplicate rules and keep checks that tfpolicy does not yet cover. tfpolicy can tell whether a resource follows platform rules. It does not necessarily know what the original ticket intended to change. For example, a ticket may only update a Storage Account tag while the Plan also replaces a database. The result might comply with resource policy and still be outside the task. Reserve -target for recovery and a

content_excerpt: Earlier this month we released GDPx , a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains: Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks. The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty. Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0 . SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com. Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. title: EVA: Evidence-seeking Visual Agent for Hallucination-Resistant Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.

title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
summary: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
summary: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.

title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
summary: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.

story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65abda82d0>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65abbf3250>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65abbf2fd0>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65ab669e90>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65ab35d990>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f65ab807110>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
